q: Explain the 'brett debate' in Châteauneuf and its stylistic stakes.
accept: traditional houses tolerate brett critics call it fault warmth low acid risk
high ph warm grenache brett risk
ans: High-pH, warm, low-acid Grenache is brett-prone; traditionalists call the barnyard note terroir, modernists call it a fault — the region's identity argument in one molecule
exp: Rayas and Beaucastel sit at the center of it, historically.

q: Crozes-Hermitage is the northern Rhône's largest cru and its most uneven. Compare its two halves and explain the consequence.
accept: the north is terraced granite and loess slopes the south is the flat chassis plain
northern sector steep and granitic southern sector alluvial galets and mechanised
gervans and larnage on slope versus beaumont-monteux and pont-de-l'isere on the plain
two halves slopes north plain south which is why quality is so uneven
ans: North of the hill — Gervans, Larnage, Crozes, Serves — the vineyards are terraced slopes on granite, loess and clay-limestone, with the famous white kaolin clay at Larnage; small, hand-worked, and capable of structure that shades toward Hermitage itself. South and east lies the Chassis plain around Beaumont-Monteux and Pont-de-l'Isère: a flat glacial terrace of rounded galets over alluvium, easily mechanised, and the source of most of the appellation's roughly 1,700 hectares. That imbalance is the consequence: one name covers both high-volume négociant wine and serious estate wine, so Crozes offers the north's best bargains and its most reliable disappointments in the same breath.
exp: Benchmarks make the point rather than settle it: Graillot and Combier work the plain to a very high standard, while Belle farms the loess and kaolin at Larnage and Chapoutier's Les Varonniers comes off the granite hillside beside Hermitage itself. Crozes expanded enormously after the 1950s and the plain absorbed nearly all of that growth — the same story as Saint-Joseph, told in different topography.

q: Walk up the Côtes du Rhône ladder, tier by tier, with the yields.
accept: cotes du rhone then villages then named villages then crus with yields falling
regional at 51 villages at 44 named commune at 41 and crus around 35 to 40
four tiers with the named-commune rung between villages and the crus
51 then 44 then 41 then the crus at thirty-five to forty hectolitres
ans: Four rungs. Côtes du Rhône, the regional appellation covering both north and south, at about 51 hl/ha. Côtes du Rhône Villages at 44. Côtes du Rhône Villages with a named commune — some twenty-odd villages including Plan de Dieu, Sablet, Séguret, Laudun, Chusclan — at 41. Then the crus, which drop the Côtes du Rhône name entirely and sit between roughly 35 and 40 hl/ha: Châteauneuf-du-Pape at 35, Gigondas at 36, the northern crus nearer 40. Yield falls at every step, along with permitted vigour and, in the crus, the right to certain varieties or colours. A named village that performs gets promoted — Vinsobres in 2006, Rasteau's dry reds in 2010, Cairanne in 2016.
exp: Candidates routinely skip the named-commune rung, which is the one the examiner is listening for. Note also what the ladder is not: a cru is a separate appellation, not a grade of Côtes du Rhône, so declassified cru fruit falls to Côtes du Rhône rather than stepping down one rung to Villages.

q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the French appellation most exposed to warming. Explain what is changing and what growers are doing about it.
accept: alcohol is climbing so growers pick earlier and lean on mourvedre cinsault and counoise
grenache ripens too fast now hence earlier harvest cooler extraction and less new oak
warming pushes alcohol past fifteen percent answered by variety choice and whole cluster
earlier harvests cooler sites more counoise and clairette concrete instead of oak
ans: Alcohols that sat near 13.5% in the 1980s now routinely reach 15% and beyond, because Grenache accumulates sugar quickly and sheds acidity faster still; harvest has advanced by two to three weeks in forty years; and drought combined with the mistral shuts stomata, stalling ripening so that phenolic and sugar maturity fall out of step. The responses run across variety, vineyard and cellar. Varietally: more Mourvèdre, Cinsault and Counoise against Grenache's dominance, and renewed interest in the neglected whites, Clairette above all. In the vineyard: earlier and parcel-by-parcel picking, retaining gobelet bush vines for their self-shading, higher trunks, no leaf-stripping on the afternoon side, cover crops for water retention, and a hard look at rootstock. In the cellar: whole-cluster fermentation, cooler and shorter extraction, concrete and amphora rather than new oak, earlier bottling. Rayas's cool sandy parcels and the higher northern sectors have gone from curiosities to templates.
exp: The 1936 minimum of 12.5%, written as an aspiration, is now a floor no one could fall through by accident — the technical argument has completely inverted in ninety years. Any master-level discussion of the southern Rhône should arrive here, and the best answers name specific levers rather than gesturing at 'climate change'.

accept: yamaoroshi mashing oxygenates cultivates lactic
yama-oroshi grinding rice for wild lactic
ans: Yama-oroshi — pole-mashing the moto to a paste so the koji enzymes dissolve the rice quickly; ambient lactic bacteria acidify the starter either way, and yamahai simply abandons the ramming ('yama-oroshi haishi')
exp: Etymology answers double as method answers.

q: Sake's koji ratios and 'tomé' additions describe which process structure?
accept: sandan jikomi three stage addition
three-step mash hatsuzoe nakazoe tomezoe
ans: San-dan jikomi: the three-stage mash build (hatsuzoe, nakazoe, tomezoe) over four days
exp: Doubling the mash stepwise keeps acidity and yeast dominance.

q: Ki-ippon, shizuku, and taruzake — define one precisely.
accept: shizuku drip pressed gravity bags
kiippon single brewery junmai shizuku gravity drip
ans: Shizuku: gravity drip through hanging bags (no press) for competition lots; ki-ippon: junmai brewed entirely at a single brewery; taruzake: cedar-cask
exp: Vocabulary depth is the oral's sake test.

q: Aged sake's chemistry: koshu's color and flavor drivers.
accept: maillard amino sugars sherry nutty
maillard reactions amber caramel soy
ans: Maillard reactions between amino acids and sugars — amber color, soy-caramel-nut depth
exp: Serve as you would Amontillado; pair with miso-caramel desserts.

crisp dry soft water northern
~light and dry
light dry
ans: 'Light and dry' — snowmelt-soft water, long cold ferments, the northern precision school
exp: Contrast Hyogo's Yamada Nishiki richness; style maps are sake's terroir.

toji is the master brewer
ans: The toji is the master brewer, historically leading seasonal crews from guilds (Nanbu, Echigo, Tajima) with distinct regional techniques
exp: Rice farmers in summer, brewers in winter — the guild schools still shape style.

q: Design a five-sake flight to teach a wine-trained palate the category.
accept: junmai daiginjo kimoto junmai nama koshu sparkling
aromatic to structural to aged
ans: A daiginjo (aromatics), a kimoto or yamahai junmai (acid and structure), a nama (freshness), a koshu (oxidative depth), and a sparkling or nigori (texture) — mapped onto wine categories the guest already knows
exp: Teach by analogy, then break the analogy.

q: Explain sake's acidity relative to wine and what follows for pairing.
accept: much lower acidity higher amino acids umami pairs with delicate
low acid high umami
ans: Far lower acidity but far higher amino acid (umami) content — so it flatters delicate and umami-rich food that acid would overwhelm, and it never fights soy or dashi
exp: The chemical reason sake succeeds where wine struggles.

q: What is 'kobo' and why do numbered yeast strains matter?
accept: yeast association numbers aroma profiles no 9 no 1801
brewing society yeast strains
ans: Kōbo is yeast; the Brewing Society's numbered strains (No. 7, No. 9, No. 1801) carry distinct aroma signatures, and a brewery's choice is a style decision
exp: No. 1801 drives the melon-apple ginjō-ka that wins competitions.

q: How should a sake list handle vintage and freshness?
accept: brewing year by rotate stock fast nama refrigerate koshu exception
freshness matters except aged
ans: Track the brewing year (BY), rotate quickly, refrigerate nama, and treat koshu as the deliberate exception — most sake is at its best within a year of shipping
exp: The opposite of a wine cellar's instincts.

q: Trace the rice from the polishing machine to the moromi: name and explain each preparatory step.
accept: polish rest wash soak steam cool then split into koji rice and kake rice
seimai karashi senmai shinseki mushimai then koji making in the muro
polishing then a rest then washing soaking steaming and division into koji and kake rice
grain is polished rested washed soaked steamed and part of it goes to the koji room
ans: Seimai, the polishing, which heats and dehydrates the grain; then karashi, a rest of days or weeks so the rice re-equilibrates with ambient moisture and stops cracking on contact with water. Senmai washes off the loosened nuka. Shinseki, the soak, is the most precisely timed operation in the brewery - for a ginjo lot it is stopwatch work over 10 kg batches, aimed at a water uptake of roughly 30% of the rice's weight and hit to within a percentage point. Mushimai steams the rice in a koshiki with rising steam, never boiling, giving the gaiko-nainan texture: firm outside, soft within. The steamed rice is cooled, then split - part goes to the muro as koji rice for roughly 48 hours of Aspergillus cultivation, the rest is kake rice fed straight into the shubo and the three-stage moromi.
exp: Steaming rather than boiling is the whole point: it gelatinises the starch while leaving the grain intact, so it dissolves at the pace the brewer chooses rather than collapsing into the mash. Every step here is a control on dissolution rate, which is the brewer's real variable - and the soak is where a percentage point of water decides how the rice behaves three weeks later.
